data.title: Analysis-Houthi advance in Yemen puts U.S. in a new bind
data.description:
Analysis-Houthi advance in Yemen puts U.S. in a new bind

By Humeyra Pamuk, Simon Lewis and Matt Spetalnick
Sat, 12 September 2026 at 1:18 pm UTC
5 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

Houthi supporters celebrate advances in Red Sea coastline

1 of 2
Houthi supporters shout slogans as they celebrate advances made by Houthi forces in fighting with government forces along Yemen's Red Sea coast, in Sanaa, Yemen, September 11, 2026. Picture taken with a mobile phone. REUTERS/Adel Al Khader

By Humeyra Pamuk, Simon Lewis and Matt Spetalnick

WASHINGTON, Sept 12 (Reuters) - A lightning offensive by the Iran-aligned Houthis has put the militants in a position to control a crucial Middle East waterway, creating a major new problem for U.S. President Donald Trump as his war with Iran grinds on in its seventh month.

Widening the Middle East conflict, Houthi fighters have advanced south along Yemen's coast, increasing their ‌ability to choke off the Bab el-Mandeb Strait — the "Gate of Tears" at the mouth of the Red Sea — giving Tehran potential leverage over both of the region's main oil-shipping corridors.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

The militants reached the island of ‌Perim on Friday, in the middle of the strait between Yemen and Africa. That is bad news for Saudi Arabia, which has been shipping much of its oil from Red Sea ports since the war effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz, on the opposite side of the Arabian Peninsula.

It also ​comes at a difficult time for Trump, who is already grappling with record-low approval ratings and searching for a way out of the conflict, most recently by announcing an economic pressure campaign designed to force concessions from Iran's government.

High U.S. gasoline prices driven by the conflict have jeopardized his Republican Party's chances of keeping control of Congress in the November midterm elections. Iran remains defiant despite being hurt militarily and economically.

"Just weeks ago, Trump adopted a strategy of squeezing Iran's economy while keeping military conflict at levels too low to squeeze the American economy," said Stephen Wertheim, a senior fellow at Carnegie Endowment for International Peace. "The Houthis have shattered Trump's plan."

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

DANGER OF JOINING THE FIGHT

The U.S. administration can't afford to have the Houthis close the strait, driving up ‌energy prices and disrupting global trade.

But at the same time, entering a fight with ⁠a foe that has withstood previous attacks by Saudi Arabia and the U.S. would be a dangerous new mission for a U.S. military already stretched by the fighting in Iran.

Saudi Arabia's de facto ruler, Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, phoned Trump on Thursday and asked for U.S. military help fighting the Houthis, three sources told Reuters. He was told Washington would not intervene ⁠directly for now but would help with intelligence, the sources said.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Trump confirmed on Saturday that he had spoken to the crown prince, and said the Houthis had also phoned his administration and asked for Washington not to become directly involved in the conflict.

A senior Trump administration official declined to address specific questions, but said the U.S. is focused on national security interests such as ensuring freedom of navigation in the Red Sea "while empowering our regional partners to take the lead in managing and resolving regional security challenges".

Saudi Arabia, Iran and ​the ​Houthis did not respond to a request for comment. Iran's foreign ministry said in a statement on Thursday that the Yemen conflict ​could not be solved by blockade or military action against the Houthis and called for ‌dialogue, without addressing Iran's own role.

A SECOND KEY STRAIT

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Iran responded to U.S. and Israeli attacks earlier this year by disrupting the Strait of Hormuz, the outlet to the Gulf through which around a fifth of global oil supplies flowed before the war.

If the Houthis close the Bab el-Mandeb, that would deal another economic blow, constraining another 7% of global petroleum supplies and about 12% of global trade.

"This was always the worst-case scenario, that the Iranians exert control not only of Strait of Hormuz but Bab el-Mandeb, two of the leading energy choke points in the world," said David Schenker, who served as Assistant Secretary of State for Near East Affairs during Trump's first term and is now at the Washington Institute for Near East Policy, a think tank.

"It's an enormous amount of leverage that [the Iranians] have in hand."

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Analysts and former officials say Trump now faces a choice: devote U.S. forces and scarce air-defense munitions to pushing back the Houthis, or leave Saudi Arabia and its allies, ‌a Yemeni government based in the south, to confront them alone.

The Houthis seized Yemen's capital 12 years ago, and a Saudi-led military ​intervention has failed to dislodge them since.

Taking on the Houthis would effectively end a deal Trump struck last year in which the U.S. would ​stop bombing the group in exchange for a halt to strikes on Red Sea shipping. That would be ​likely to expose U.S. forces to missile attacks from Yemen.

A STRETCHED U.S. MILITARY

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

It would also be another burden for the U.S. military.

U.S. officials say a fight with the Houthis could require significant ‌naval and aerial resources and divert U.S. intelligence assets, given the need to pinpoint Houthi ​positions that have changed since last year.

If U.S. Navy vessels ​and aircraft have to start shooting down Houthi drones and missiles, it could also worsen diminished stockpiles of U.S. munitions and air-defense interceptors.

The senior administration official denied that the U.S. was concerned about its resources being stretched. "The United States Military has more than enough munitions, ammo, and stockpiles to serve all of the Commander-in-Chief's strategic goals and beyond," the official said.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Tim Lenderking, who served as U.S. special envoy on Yemen under former President Joe ​Biden and is now a principal at law firm Squire Patton Boggs, said that ‌with Trump signaling an unwillingness to get directly involved militarily against the Houthis, the U.S. needs to do more to share intelligence with the Saudis for their air campaign and step up diplomatic and material ​support for Yemen's internationally recognized government.

"This administration came in asking the question, 'What can Yemen do for us?'" Lenderking said during a webcast sponsored by the Middle East Institute think-tank in Washington. "Well, Yemen can spoil ​our day."

(Reporting by Humeyra Pamuk, Simon Lewis and Matt Spetalnick; additional reporting by Idrees Ali, Jonathan Landay and Timour Azheri)

data.title: President Trump says Irish reunification ‘would be a fantastic thing,’ during visit to Ireland
data.description:
President Trump says Irish reunification ‘would be a fantastic thing,’ during visit to Ireland

Kit Maher, Issy Ronald, Niamh Kennedy, CNN
Sat, 12 September 2026 at 12:16 pm UTC
8 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

President Donald Trump said Saturday that Irish reunification "would be a fantastic thing" during a bilateral meeting with Ireland's Taoiseach Micheál Martin, something he projected is "going to happen eventually."

When a reporter asked his view on the topic, Trump at first acknowledged his comments could inflame a politically sensitive issue before voicing support.

"Well, I don't want to cause any trouble," Trump said Saturday. "But I will tell you, I'd love to see it unified," arguing it would be "a great feather in everybody's cap."

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

The reunification of Ireland has long been considered a contentious issue, dividing opinion among the Unionists, typically from Protestant backgrounds, who would like Northern Ireland to remain part of the United Kingdom and Republicans, typically from Catholic backgrounds, who would like to see it reunited with the Republic of Ireland.

For nearly 30 years, Northern Ireland was plagued by significant sectarian violence and disorder, in a period known as the Troubles. Under the US-brokered 1997 'Good Friday' agreement which brought peace to the province, a majority of voters in border polls held both in the north and south would need to be in favor of reunification for this to take place. Wary of such sensitivities, US presidents have typically avoided explicitly commenting on the issue, even President Joe Biden who frequently referenced his Irish heritage.

Trump's comments were almost immediately met with pushback from the UK government and unionists. Downing Street pointed CNN to newly installed UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham's comments in August when he downplayed the prospect of an imminent border poll in Northern Ireland. That is currently "off the table," he said, later confirming he would "100%" follow the Good Friday Agreement.

Gavin Robinson, who leads the Democratic Unionist Party, said that Northern Ireland's future "will be decided by the people of Northern Ireland, not by commentary in London, Dublin or Washington."

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

However, Trump seemed confident that the move would happen eventually and questioned how it could be a negative thing.

"It's going to happen eventually. … I think it will happen now. You've got the right man over here to get it moving," Trump said, pointing at Martin. "But yeah, I think it would be a fantastic thing. Now the UK will have something to say about obviously, but I think it would be a great thing. I mean, how can it be bad?"

Trump touched down in Ireland Saturday morning, to hold talks with the country's leaders before attending a tournament at one of his golf courses.

Trump's son, Donald Trump Jr. and his wife, Bettina, disembarked from the plane afterward and also greeted officials on the ground.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

During the visit, Trump heard an Irish band play the American national anthem, immediately followed by the Irish anthem, while Irish President Catherine Connolly stood by expressionless. Trump briefly answered a couple questions on his way back into the Beast after the courtesy call with Connolly, including one concerning traffic through the Bab al-Mandeb strait.

"Everything will work out just fine. It's all going to work out fine," Trump said.

The last time Trump visited Ireland as president was during his first term in June 2019. This visit takes Trump out the US at a crucial time for him politically, just weeks before the midterms and as the Iran-backed Houthis' rapid advance in Yemen threatens to open a second front in the war with Iran.

During his time in Ireland, Trump will largely be shielded from the public and kept away from expected protests. Instead, he will be ferried by motorcade straight to three official government residences in Phoenix Park, a huge urban park in central Dublin which officials have closed since Friday night.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

There, he will hold a bilateral meeting with Taoiseach Micheál Martin and deliver remarks to business leaders at US Ambassador to Ireland Edward Walsh's residence, a White House official told CNN.

The president's meetings with Irish political leaders will touch on bilateral economic cooperation, creating business opportunities for US industry, and discussing international issues of mutual interest, the official said.

Expected protests

Trump's visit presents a tricky balancing act for the Irish government. On the one hand, US companies, many of whom have their European headquarters in Ireland, are hugely important for the country's economy while, on the other, Trump remains unpopular with much of the Irish public and some protests are expected.

Alongside a demonstration planned for Saturday afternoon in central Dublin, protests are also expected to take place in Doonbeg, the village in the west of Ireland where Trump's golf course is located and also at Shannon Airport.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Numerous protests have been held by anti-war activist groups at the airport over the years protesting the US military's use of the facility as a refueling stop for its troops.

Back in 1984, then-President Ronald Reagan's visit to Ireland was marked by protests. Archival footage from RTÉ News shows thousands participating in a "ring around Reagan" protest, including anti-nuclear groups. "REFUSE CRUISE" was written on makeshift missiles and video shows a banner with "$ FOR WANT NOT FOR WAR" written on it.

Asked about the planned protests against his visit in Ireland, Trump said he was unaware of them.

"I didn't know there was a protest," Trump said. "It can't be a very big one, because we've been all over Ireland today already," though he had just landed in Dublin a couple hours prior.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

"I haven't seen any protest. It's a friendly protest," he added. "But we have a great relationship with Ireland."

CNN photojournalist William Bonnett captured a small group of about 20 to 30 protestors in Doonbeg and Shannon Saturday morning. One woman held a sign that read, "We do not like you here nor there. We do not like you ANYWHERE!" Another person held a sign with the words "CRUEL, CORRUPT, COWARDLY" splashed in red over Trump's face and another "NO FAUX-KING WELCOME."

After wrapping up his meetings in Dublin, Trump will head west on Sunday to his Doonbeg course where he will attend the Irish Open tournament.

His son, Eric, told Irish national broadcaster RTÉ that the golf course is the largest employer in the local area.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

"Go down to Morrissey's tavern in Doonbeg and hear from a real Irish person as to whether or not they like President Trump and the Trump family," he said. "Go have them attest to what we've done for the country and what we've invested in the country and the love and respect that our family has always shown them."

Connolly was among those who protested Trump's visit in 2019 before she was elected to the ceremonial position of Ireland's president in 2025. Hosting Martin in the Oval Office for a visit on St. Patrick's Day in March, Trump referred to Connolly as a "he" when asked by an Irish reporter about her comments about "violations of international law" in the Middle East.

"Look, he's lucky I exist, that's all I can say," Trump said. "If you're gonna allow countries that are sick and demented – and they are demented – to have nuclear weapons–everybody in the whole world should be very thankful."

If there was any tension between Connolly and Trump, he didn't hint at it, calling her "terrific" during his remarks at the embassy later.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Trump seemed aware that his visit was bound to generate headlines. Later Saturday, he joked about how the reporter who asked him about Irish reunification put him in a tough spot, aware that his answer made news.

"I think we'll read about it tomorrow. That's one of those questions where, no matter what you say, no matter how well you say it, there's no good answer, right?" Trump said during remarks at the US Embassy.

"But I actually said it would be, I think, a very cool thing. To be honest with you, I think it would be cool, as half the room clears out," Trump said, prompting laughter.

While Trump said he hates "what's happening with Europe" on immigration and trade, he gave effusive praise to the people of Ireland, the only English-speaking nation in the European Union with somewhat of a backhanded compliment about their toughness.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

"People love coming to Ireland. You know why? Because they love you. They love the people. There's a friendliness. There's, uh, there's also a vicious and a toughness," Trump said. "Let me tell you, you are some of the most vicious bastards I've ever (seen). But when you want to be nice, there's nobody nicer."

This story has been updated with additional developments.

data.title: Zelensky open to meeting Putin at G20 in Miami
data.description:
Zelensky open to meeting Putin at G20 in Miami

AFP News
Sat, 12 September 2026 at 12:55 pm UTC
4 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said he would be willing to meet Russian leader Vladimir Putin at the G20 summit in Miami for talks on ending the war, in a media interview released Saturday.

The Kremlin said it has not yet made a decision on whether Putin would attend the gathering of world leaders in December, and repeated the Russian leader's demand that Zelensky come to Russia for talks.

Washington is seeking to kick-start long-stalled negotiations to find a solution to the conflict, Europe's deadliest since World War II, with US negotiators recently visiting Kyiv and Moscow and President Donald Trump and Putin this week holding talks on the conflict over the phone.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

The United States holds this year's presidency of the Group of 20 major economies, which comprises 19 countries plus the European Union and the African Union, and culminates in the December 14-15 leaders' summit.

Russia's finance minister has already attended a G20 meeting, causing discomfort among some of Ukraine's European allies, and a Russian delegation is set to take part in an energy ministers' gathering next week.

Asked whether he would be willing to meet Putin at the December summit if both leaders were invited, Zelensky told German broadcaster Deutsche Welle: "Yes, of course.

"We have to come. We have to meet, to speak, and make decisions. It's not about words. What I will tell him or what he wants to tell me, it doesn't matter."

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

All that mattered were "results", he added.

But Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov was cited by Russia's TASS news agency as saying that "we do not know yet whether we will be going to Miami".

Peskov repeated Putin's demand that Zelensky come to Russia -- which launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, triggering the war -- for any talks: "If he really wants to meet Putin, then Putin has said before that he can fly to Moscow."

Last weekend, US negotiators Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner visited Moscow and Putin and Trump also discussed the war during the week in what the Kremlin termed an "extremely frank" and constructive hour-long phone call.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

In the Deutsche Welle interview, which took place Friday in Canada, Zelensky said that Witkoff and Kushner's visit was a "good signal", and it was important the pair had visited Kyiv as well as Moscow.

"It's respect to our people," he said.

Zelensky has also announced he plans to meet Trump in late September, as Washington pushes for fresh face-to-face talks between Moscow and Kyiv.

- 'Good position for talks' -

Asked about Ukraine's position ahead of possible negotiations, Zelensky responded: "Ukraine now is much more stronger than last year on the battlefield.

"That's why we think that we have now (a) good position for negotiations."

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Kyiv has said the talks could happen as early as this month, but the Kremlin on Monday said it was "too early" to discuss a venue or dates.

Several previous rounds of negotiations have failed. Trust between the sides is low, and there is no sign that Moscow or Kyiv have shifted their positions.

Both Moscow and Kyiv have escalated long-range strikes on each other in recent months, leading to the highest civilian death toll since the early days of the war.

Overnight Russian strikes killed four people in Ukraine, including two in Zaporizhzhia in the south and two at an ArcelorMittal plant in central Kryvyi Rih, local authorities and the steelmaker said Saturday.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

In the southern port city of Odesa, Russian missile and drone strikes hit residential buildings, destroying entire floors and leaving 35 people injured, the regional governor said.

In the interview, Zelensky also repeated his call for Ukraine's allies to provide more missiles to fend off Russian air attacks.

Ukraine urgently needs more interceptor missiles for US-made Patriot air defence systems, but US supplies have been reduced after Washington used large numbers during its war with Iran.

It was not clear whether Washington would provide enough missiles, said Zelensky, adding that they have "political will to sell and to help, but the production is not too big".

He also urged greater help from European allies: "All the Europeans who really support us have what we need."

data.title: French police suspect train derailment was sabotage
data.description:
French police suspect train derailment was sabotage

Guillaume Saligot, with Benjamin Massot in Rennes and Sabine Colpart in Paris
Sat, 12 September 2026 at 12:41 pm UTC
2 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

French investigators suspect sabotage was behind a train derailment in northwestern France that injured 44 people and left passengers in a state of shock, prosecutors said on Saturday.

Carrying 186 passengers, the train was running between the Normandy cities of Rouen and Caen when it came off the rails around 7:45 pm (1745 GMT) Friday close to Renault's factory in the town of Cleon.

During the derailment, one carriage tipped onto its side while four others left the tracks.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

A fragment of rail was found on the track, with the possibility of a malicious act being treated as the main line of inquiry, said Rouen prosecutor Sebastien Gallois.

"The reasons for its presence are unknown and will have to be determined by the investigation," he said.

Tests for drugs and alcohol on the train driver had come back negative.

Authorities activated a mass-casualty response plan, with 130 firefighters, five medical teams and 80 vehicles drafted in.

An AFP photographer saw a mass of railway staff working around the train on Saturday morning.

Gallois said 44 people were injured including an 18-year-old woman evacuated "in a critical condition".

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

She was no longer in life-threatening condition on Saturday but remained hospitalised.

- 'Really shocking' -

Cleon mayor Melanie Delacour said the victims were "in a state of shock."

"The windows of the carriages that remained upright shattered, and because of the train's speed, stones flew into the carriages," she told AFP.

She said that some victims had told her they would never take the train again.

"It is a tragedy that could have turned into a disaster on a very large scale," Delacour added.

One of the passengers said the accident was "really shocking."

"Suddenly there were a few jolts, and then after about three seconds it got stronger and stronger," Louis, 24, told ICI Normandie radio.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

"I couldn't stay in my seat any more," he said. "The windows partially shattered, the stones from the track came into the carriage," he said.

"I'm still shaking," he added.

SNCF Reseau, which controls the French rail network, initially said that traffic on the line had been suspended and power to the tracks cut to allow emergency services to operate.

According to SNCF, the accident caused "major disruptions" to rail traffic between Rouen and Caen and between Caen and Le Havre in both directions.

A spokesperson for SNCF Reseau said on Saturday that services had resumed.

The train will only be lifted off the line once the public prosecutor allows it, with investigations into the cause of the derailment still ongoing.

SNCF said that it would offer "full cooperation in complete transparency" to the inquiry.

data.title: Trump says Iran likely responsible for attack on vital Saudi oil pipeline
data.description:
Trump says Iran likely responsible for attack on vital Saudi oil pipeline

Sophie Tanno, CNN
Sat, 12 September 2026 at 12:18 pm UTC
3 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

US President Donald Trump said Iran was "probably" behind the attack on a vital oil pipeline in Saudi Arabia which led to its closure.

The East-West Pipeline was attacked by several drones coming from Iraq on Thursday, the Saudi foreign ministry said Friday, resulting in injuries and some damage. The energy ministry added that the pipeline had been shut down as a precautionary measure.

The news comes amid turmoil in energy markets and major disruption in shipping with no end in sight to the Iran war and as Tehran's allies in Yemen, the Houthis, seized a key island and a port in the Red Sea.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Trump pointed the finger at Iran as most likely being behind the attack when asked about the incident by a reporter during a visit to Ireland on Saturday.

"I think they are, probably they are," Trump told journalists in Dublin.

It remains unclear at this stage who was behind the attacks. A key umbrella group of Iran-backed militias in Iraq, known as the Islamic Resistance in Iraq, has denied responsibility.

The attack is another headache for Saudi Arabia, which has been backing Yemen's internationally recognized government against the Houthis.

Trump said he had held a call with Saudi Crown ​Prince Mohammed bin Salman, whom he referred to ​as ‌a "good friend."

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

A source told CNN that the Saudi Crown Prince had spoken twice with Trump on Thursday and urged him to strike the Houthis as the Iran-backed group advances towards the Red Sea, but Trump declined.

Responding to a question about the fresh concerns in Saudi Arabia following the closure of the pipeline, and whether he could help move marine traffic through the Strait of Hormuz in light of the developments, Trump said everything will "work out fine."

The White House, in response to CNN's questions about the calls, said that the US was in touch with the Saudis and "focused on protecting our core national security interests— such as ensuring freedom of navigation in the Red Sea — while empowering our regional partners to take the lead in managing and resolving regional security challenges."

Borders close in Iraq

Saudi Arabia's Ministry of Energy statement said the pipeline "was subjected to multiple attacks" on Thursday that "resulted in a number of injuries." The statement added that teams were "taking the necessary measures to secure the pipeline and assess its safety."

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

The Iraqi government condemned the attacks, saying it had ordered an urgent investigation into those responsible and that it will not allow its territory or airspace to be used for such purposes.

On Saturday, Iraqi authorities said the country has closed a number of its borders as a precautionary measure.

The strike and recent Houthi advances along the Red Sea signal that Saudi Arabia's oil resources — and its ability to export those resources — are facing increasing threats as the Iran war continues.

Saudi Arabia's East-West Pipeline has become vital for the country to maintain oil exports since the outbreak of the US-Iran war.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

The kingdom has rerouted about 5 million barrels of oil per day that would have been destined for awaiting oil tankers in the Persian Gulf, as Iran effectively shuttered the Strait of Hormuz. Instead, that oil has traveled through the pipeline to Saudi Arabia's port of Yanbu on the Red Sea.

This story has been updated with additional information.

CNN's Kylie Atwood, Katie Bo Lillis, Thomas Bordeaux and Zachary Cohen contributed to this report.

For more CNN news and newsletters create an account at CNN.com

data.title: BRICS adopts joint declaration, urges 'maximum restraint' in Mideast
data.description:
BRICS adopts joint declaration, urges 'maximum restraint' in Mideast

By Sarita Chaganti Singh
Sat, 12 September 2026 at 12:13 pm UTC
1 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

By Sarita Chaganti Singh

NEW DELHI, Sept 12 (Reuters) - The BRICS group of nations unanimously adopted a ‌joint declaration on Saturday, expressing "deep concern" over the war ‌in the Middle East and urged maximum restraint, advocating for a "multilateral ​approach" that respects national viewpoints.

The declaration, adopted on the first day of the BRICS leaders' annual summit in New Delhi, comes at a time when U.S. and Iran have ‌resumed tit-for-tat strikes ⁠against each other, after a pause in fighting for much of August.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

The BRICS bloc includes ⁠both Iran and Washington-ally United Arab Emirates, which was expected to make clinching a joint statement consensus a particularly ​challenging task ​for host New Delhi.

"We express ​deep concern over the ‌continued escalation of tensions in Middle East...call for exercising maximum restraint...avoiding actions that could further aggravate the situation," the 'New Delhi Declaration' said.

The declaration also reiterated the commitment of member nations to a peaceful resolution of international disputes "through ‌dialogue, consultation, and diplomacy".

In addition, they ​voiced concerns about the rise ​of "unilateral tariff and non-tariff ​measures" that distort trade, against the backdrop ‌of U.S. sanctions against Tehran ​amid its war ​with the country, and against Russia over its conflict with Ukraine.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

BRICS includes Brazil, Russia, India, China, South ​Africa, Egypt, Ethiopia, ‌Indonesia, Iran and the United Arab Emirates.

(Reporting by ​Hritam Mukherjee and Shilpa Jamkhandikar, writing by Sakshi ​Dayal; Editing by YP Rajesh)

data.title: Farage's Reform UK receives second £36 million pound donation from crypto investor
data.description:
Farage's Reform UK receives second £36 million pound donation from crypto investor

Reuters
Sat, 12 September 2026 at 12:04 pm UTC
1 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

FILE PHOTO: Reform UK party conference, in Birmingham

1 of 2
FILE PHOTO: Britain's Reform UK party leader and MP for Clacton, Nigel Farage speaks during the Reform UK party conference, in Birmingham, Britain, September 5, 2026. REUTERS/Temilade Adelaja/File Photo

LONDON, Sept 12 (Reuters) - Britain's Reform UK has received a £36 million ($48.66 million)donation from cryptocurrency billionaire ‌Christopher Harborne, giving Nigel Farage's party its ‌second huge contribution in the space of two days as it ​gears up for the next general election.

Harborne, Reform's biggest donor, said in an article published by the Telegraph newspaper on Saturday that he had matched a ‌record £36 million donation ⁠announced on Friday by fellow cryptocurrency entrepreneur Ben Delo.

"A strong country is one that ⁠is funded by a vigorous economy which is creating jobs. That's why I'm putting my money into ​what I ​believe is the only ​viable cause which will ‌get the job of regeneration done," Harborne wrote in the newspaper.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

"My view is that Nigel Farage and the party fully understand what a government needs to do to get our country back on the ‌right track.

"Whilst I have been ​making donations to Reform of ​around £1m a month, ​Ben Delo told me he was ‌going to make a record ​donation of £36 million. ​My competitive spirit inspired me to match it, so that is what I've done," Harbone ​said.

The donations amount ‌to £72 million in funding for the party ​over 48 hours.

($1 = 0.7398 pounds)

data.title: Congress Is Starting To Argue About A Potential AI Apocalypse
data.description:
Congress Is Starting To Argue About A Potential AI Apocalypse

Arthur Delaney
Sat, 12 September 2026 at 12:00 pm UTC
4 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

WASHINGTON — Lawmakers are not exactly rushing to prevent tech companies from endangering humanity's existence with rogue autonomous software, but recent warnings from industry insiders are prompting real debate, and potentially even action, sooner rather than later.

Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas), chair of the Senate Commerce Committee, has been working on a bill with Sen. Amy Klobuchar (D-Minn.) and Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) on legislation to address the potentially "catastrophic risk" artificial intelligence poses. But at least one key Democrat fears the legislation isn't strong enough, warning it could be used to block more meaningful action at the state level.

Politics: She Watched Federal Agents Kill Alex Pretti. Now She Has Told Investigators What She Saw.

Still, the apocalyptic visions emanating from the tech industry have injected new urgency into negotiations that have been ongoing for weeks.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

"It's clear we need to act now and not wait," Klobuchar said Friday in a statement to HuffPost about the legislation, which would give the government some form of oversight over companies' AI models. "I'm continuing to work toward a bipartisan agreement on legislation for government oversight of the greatest risks posed by AI models."

Klobuchar said one goal would be to require developers to work with government experts to verify and test their models to make sure they're safe.

"We cannot allow the release of dangerous models, including those that evade the control of their developers," Klobuchar said.

Politics: Here's A Video Of Trump At The 25th Anniversary 9/11 Ceremony

The committee's top Democrat, Sen. Maria Cantwell (D-Wash.), panned the Cruz-Klobuchar effort on social media on Thursday evening, calling their policy "a weak federal standard" that would prevent states from enacting tougher protections.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

The bill hasn't been introduced, but Cantwell's message suggested part of it could be similar, in a "backdoor" way, to Cruz's proposal from last year to enact a 10-year moratorium banning states from enacting their own AI rules. The Senate jettisoned the proposal from its big tax bill last year amid opposition from Republicans, but Cruz has insisted it would come back.

"Republicans are suddenly waking up to the urgent need for tough AI safety rules, a sharp reversal from last year when House Republicans and Chairman Cruz tried to impose a 10-year moratorium on state AI regulations that the tech bros wanted," Cantwell said.

Thune's involvement means an eventual bill could have significant Republican support, since he's the party's leader in the Senate.

Politics: Conservative Legal Icon Warns Trump Plans To 'Wage The Final Battle' Against Democracy

The politics of AI has shifted dramatically in the last two weeks. Disclosures from AI companies revealed swarms of their "agents" escaped what were supposed to be closed internal systems and monkeyed around on public websites, and this week a researcher at Anthropic resigned, accusing both Anthropic and OpenAI of endangering humanity by developing potentially superintelligent AI programs they can't control.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) has called for an immediate pause on advanced AI development — an idea that's not currently on the table in Congress, but one Sanders predicted would become more popular.

"How in God's name can you keep going forward in the direction of superintelligence when you don't know what that means?" Sanders told HuffPost. "So I think the idea of a pause is going to generate more and more interest and more and more support."

Cruz is broadly aligned with AI industry leaders and their White House allies, who have argued against heavy regulations on the technology, suggesting limiting its potential would allow Chinese AI companies to gain an edge. On Thursday, he suggested on social media that Sanders' proposals were created at the behest of the Chinese Communist Party.

Politics: Trump Floods Truth Social With Bizarre Posts On 9/11 Anniversary

Speaking on The View this week, Cruz said the risks posed by AI are indeed "frightening." He said his still-being-written legislation would require "government supervision and approval" of AI models. Cruz, Klobuchar and Thune have been at odds over exactly how intrusive the government's AI oversight would be. Asked if Congress would eventually pass a bill, Cruz seemed to want to manage expectations.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

"It is possible, but it ain't easy," he said. "This is a very divided time."

data.title: Trump says he would 'love' to see a united Ireland
data.description:
Trump says he would 'love' to see a united Ireland

By Bo Erickson, Padraic Halpin and Conor Humphries
Sat, 12 September 2026 at 11:55 am UTC
3 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

U.S. President Donald Trump visits Ireland

1 of 11
U.S. President Donald Trump meets with Ireland's Prime Minister (Taoiseach) Micheal Martin at Farmleigh House in Dublin, Ireland, September 12, 2026. REUTERS/Kylie Cooper

By Bo Erickson, Padraic Halpin and Conor Humphries

DUBLIN, Sept 12 (Reuters) - U.S. President Donald Trump said on Saturday he would "love" to see British-run Northern Ireland unify with Ireland, remarks made during a visit to Dublin that drew a ‌sharp response from pro-British unionists in Northern Ireland.

Trump's comments come weeks after new British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said a referendum ‌on Northern Ireland leaving the United Kingdom was "off the table", a position Downing Street on Saturday said remained unchanged.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

"Well, I don't want to cause any problems, but I ​will tell you, I'd love to see it unified," Trump told reporters sitting next to Irish Prime Minister Micheal Martin after the pair met in Dublin. "It's going to happen eventually ... I think it would be a fantastic thing."

'A VERY COOL THING'

"Now the UK will have something to say about it ... but I think it would be a great thing," he added.

Trump later said that there "was no good answer" to the question on ‌Irish unity but repeated that he thought it ⁠would be "a very cool thing".

Under the terms of the 1998 Good Friday Agreement, a referendum on Northern Ireland leaving the UK can be held only at the discretion of the British government. The accord ended three ⁠decades of violence between Irish nationalists seeking a united Ireland and unionists who wanted Northern Ireland to remain part of the UK.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

While polls show a comfortable majority in Northern Ireland favour remaining in the UK, the gap has narrowed slightly since Britain's departure from the European Union pushed unity higher ​up the ​political agenda.

The leader of Northern Ireland's largest unionist party, the Democratic Unionist ​Party, rejected Trump's prediction, saying unification would lead to "the ‌destruction of our country."

"Northern Ireland's constitutional future will be decided by the people of Northern Ireland, not by commentary in London, Dublin or Washington," Gavin Robinson, who has publicly supported Trump in the past, wrote on X.

Previous U.S. presidents, including those with strong Irish heritage like Joe Biden, have been careful to remain neutral on Irish unification. The U.S. government played a key role in brokering the 1998 peace deal.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

'YOU FLEECED US'

Trump is making the 48-hour trip as his Republican Party campaigns to retain its majorities in both chambers of the U.S. Congress. He is ‌due to attend a golf tournament at one of his resorts later on ​Saturday.

Trump also met Irish President Catherine Connolly, who was elected head of state last year. ​When Trump last visited Ireland as president in 2019, ​Connolly, an outspoken politician with far-left foreign policy views, protested outside Shannon Airport in western Ireland.

Anti-war and anti-Trump protests ‌are planned in Dublin on Saturday and in western Ireland ​near the Trump International Golf Links ​in Doonbeg.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Martin focused his remarks on the countries' close economic ties. U.S.-owned companies, mainly in the technology and pharmaceutical sectors, employ about 10% of workers in Ireland after successive governments prioritized their jobs and tax dollars over decades.

"You took all our medical ​companies, we've got to get a couple of ‌them back," Trump said.

"You fleeced us but that's okay... There's a lot of room to go around and our ​relationship with you is fantastic."

(Reporting by Bo Erickson, Padraic Halpin and Conor Humphries in Dublin, Will James and Sam ​Tabahriti in London; Editing by Rod Nickel, Peter Graff and Mark Potter)

data.title: Trump says Irish unification would be 'fantastic'
data.description:
Trump says Irish unification would be 'fantastic'

Peter Hutchison, Aurelia End and Peter Murphy
Sat, 12 September 2026 at 11:42 am UTC
4 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

Donald Trump said Saturday he would "love to see" a united Ireland, wading into a politically sensitive subject as he embarked on a two-day Irish visit that blurs the lines between his presidency and personal business interests.

After meeting Ireland's Prime Minister Micheal Martin in Dublin, Trump said reunification of the Republic of Ireland and Northern Ireland -- split for over a century -- would be "a fantastic thing".

"The way I look at it, it's going to happen eventually. It may as well happen now," he told reporters, adding though that "the UK will have something to say about it, obviously".

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

The island of Ireland has been split between the Irish republic in the south and Northern Ireland, which is part of the United Kingdom, since 1921.

Under the 1998 Good Friday Agreement, which ended three decades of sectarian violence in Northern Ireland that killed about 3,000 people, a referendum can be held if the UK government determines a majority there is likely to favour joining the Republic of Ireland.

The people of the Republic of Ireland would also have to vote in favour for reunification to occur.

The United States has previously adopted a position of neutrality on the issue.

UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham insisted last month that a unity referendum was "off the table", drawing a sharp response from the pro-unity party Sinn Fein.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

"As unionists we are not interested in the destruction of our country by joining with the Irish Republic," Gavin Robinson, leader of the pro-British Democratic Unionist Party, said on X in response to Trump's comments.

- Divergences -

The US president touched down at Dublin airport in his Qatari-gifted plane shortly before 8:25 am (0725 GMT) under a security operation dubbed one of the largest ever mounted in Ireland.

At least 4,000 police and other personnel, including snipers, are mobilised for the visit, which will see Trump fly to his luxury resort in Doonbeg on Ireland's west coast to watch the Irish Open golf tournament.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

He inspected a military guard of honour after being received by left-wing President Catherine Connolly, an outspoken critic of the US leader.

He then met Martin, when the Iran war and US tariffs on EU pharmaceuticals and immigration were on the agenda.

Ireland and the United States have long been close allies, partly because of their common ancestral ties.

But the Irish government's politics diverge sharply from those of the Trump administration on many issues, with Ireland being one of Europe's most pro-Palestinian countries.

Ireland is among several countries, including Spain, the UK and France, that have announced a trade ban targeting Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

After a brief visit to the US embassy, Trump was due to fly to his Doonbeg resort -- a remote, coastal site in County Clare that the Trump Organization purchased in 2014.

- 'Private interests' -

His attendance at the Irish Open adds an extra layer of complexity to a security effort that is reportedly costing Ireland 20 million euros ($23 million).

It comes with the country already grappling with a massive policing operation for its six-month presidency of the EU.

Some 40,000 fans are expected at the tournament over the weekend, with six-time major winner and current world number two Rory McIlroy the main draw.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

McIlroy, who has played golf with Trump, told the BBC this week that the tournament will feel "different" with the US president on site, but that the players will just "keep our heads down and play".

The 80-year-old billionaire has promoted his family's golf business unabashedly since returning to the White House for his second stint as president in January 2025.

Last summer, he welcomed then-UK Prime Minister Keir Starmer and European Union chief Ursula von der Leyen to his plush resort at Turnberry on the west coast of Scotland.

Trump then inaugurated another golf course bearing his name in the town of Balmedie, near Aberdeen on the northeast Scottish coast.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

The golf-mad president -- whose relaxed relationship with the game's rules was documented by sports journalist Rick Reilly in the 2019 book "Commander in Cheat" -- may even award the trophy on Sunday.

"He's really just visiting the golf resort he owns and dropping into Dublin for a courtesy visit," Daniel Geary, a US history professor at Trinity College Dublin, told AFP.

"He sees little difference between his private interests and his role as president."
